utterances.text: Well, I assume that Mr. Arif Pasalic knows the situation better than I do because he sign the document. So I don't want to comment on that further. We've seen the document and I'll move on. You've already said today, sir, and you said it yesterday, that during 1992, within the composition of the BH armed forces, there was also the Territorial Defence and the HVO and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Since they were jointly in the -- in this composition, I assume that they shared responsibilities, duties, or you tried to do that wherever that was possible?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were attempts to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that will be sufficient. Now may we have on e-court the following document. It is P 00385, and you will have it in your bundle. You have the numbers at the side. P 00385. While we're waiting for the document to appear, it is an order from the military police administration. It is dated the 12th of August, 1992, and signed by the chief Valentin Coric. That is what it says in printed letters, but his deputy signed it, but that's not important. I'd like to read out the first paragraph once again which reads as follows: "I hereby order that in the municipalities of Herzegovina, controlled by the Croatian Defence Council, apart from the municipalities of Mostar, Konjic, Jablanica, and Gornji Vakuf, that permission for vehicles to move around and members of the TO BiH on the territory of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna should be issued by commanders of the military police posts of the corresponding municipalities on the basis of assessing the justifications for the travel permit." From this document we can see, and I think that you'll agree with me there, that the municipalities quote where the HVO municipalities did not issue permits, the municipalities of Mostar, Konjic, Jablanica and Gornji Vakuf are the ones mentioned. Now, the municipalities that I've just read out, are they municipalities that were characteristic by the fact that they had an ethnically-mixed population and some of them had a majority Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Would it then emerge from this that it is most probable that in those municipalities that were inhabited or, rather, the person issuing the permits assumed that permits of this kind in those municipalities would be issued by the authorities which were in charge of the Territorial Defence. And in this case, those would be the authorities or municipal boards in which the representatives of the Muslims were in power. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Who issued these permits then? Who took care about where people were going, where there was a majority population -- Muslim population and where there were check-points of the Territorial Defence? Who saw to that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody was a recruit.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody was a recruit and wanted to leave the area, leave the territory, not because of the HVO check-points but because of the BH army check-points, for one to be able to move around, for example, someone might have spent 10 or 15 days on duty there and then had -- wanted to go back on leave. Now, in order to ensure that our army check-points didn't prevent such people from passing through them and ensuring that these people were not deserters, only in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I wanted to ask you and hear from you although I might not have been clear enough. Now, my next question is as follows: In Jablanica in 1992, as far as I was able to understand you at the same time, we had the existence of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was also the Territorial Defence in existence with its own military police, and there was the military police of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, how many members did this MUP have, the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you know, if not say so?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it had almost 200 members.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the Territorial Defence, how many members did it have?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about one and a half thousand people.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And the TO military police?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police had people from the corps. For example, 50 at most from our municipality. The military police was established at the level -- at corps level.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And you said it had around 50 members?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know how many members the HVO in Jablanica had headed by Mr. Livaja?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 30 men, unless I'm very much mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, you're not very much mistaken. That's right. Now, tell me, please, do you know whether the HVO had their military police or the Territorial Defence military police, whether they had a crime department, or was that the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP had a crime department. I can't really say. In different periods of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I have already many times told you please, do not kill the interpreters -- said kill all the lawyers but now we don't want to kill the interpreters. So, please, kindly wait for each other to finish and then to speak. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: You haven't answered me about the crime department that I asked you.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, I'm not quite sure that it existed within the military police. It -- that kind of department existed within the MUP. Later on -- well, no, I really can't say. I can't answer that question because that formation was something I never liked very much, I mean the military police. I never liked any military police. They were all of very doubtful morals, and they engendered problems. So I kept a wide breast of them -- wide berth of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document later on and I'm going to remind you of who the members of the military police were. Now, in answer to a question from my colleague Ms. Alaburic, you mentioned Zuka's units and then the Silver Foxes, or Srebrni Lisicit, then Cedo's units and the Wolves, et cetera. What I'm interested in, first, before I go in to ask you about any of these, is that the Green Berets turned up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: At the head of these -- Hanefija Prijic, nicknamed Paraga, was he at the head of those Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Were these Green Berets just as problematic as all the others or not?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether these same Green Berets already in June, 1992, caused various incidents by shooting from automatic weapons in front of the military police building, for instance? That happened on the 19th of June 1992. Do you know about that incident?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Zuka's units, when they arrived, you told us on several occasions that you testified in the Tuta and Stela trial, so I took a look at what you said there, your testimony there. So I'd like to refresh your memory, rather, ask you whether you remember that when you testified there you said that Zuka's unit numbered about 400 men.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I didn't know the exact figure, but when it was up to full strength, they had about 350 to 400 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think that in that same statement of yours, apart from all the problems that were raised today linked to them, it was also stated that the members of that unit would evict Croats from their houses and flats and that they would move into them, take up residence in those same houses. That's what you said in Tuta and Stela, so I'm asking you now.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said yesterday, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me whether you remember that that kind of thing happened?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably did happen. Things like that probably did happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's enough for me. Thank you. Now tell me this: Do you happen to know that these Zuka's unit -- units or unit, among other things, evicted the HVO military police from their building. Do you know about that incident?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't say that that did not happen, but I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: When in Tuta and Stela you said that the Main Staff commanded Zuka's unit and that they were more numerous and better armed than you, better trained than you and better equipped than you, younger and stronger than you --

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: -- that you were not able to stand up to them, that you were no match for them.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to repeat. It was called a special detachment for special assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to repeat. I apologise for interrupting, but just tell me if my conclusion is the right one, that you were simply no match for them?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. So apart from these Zuka's units, you also had another -- you also had problems with refugees from Jajce, from Prozor, from Eastern Bosnia, Foca. You also mentioned that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Right, then, but Prozor in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Eastern Herzegovina, from Eastern Bosnia, especially from Foca. They came from all parts. And quite a lot from our own refugees from Jablanica, from Doljani, Sovici, Slatina and Prozor. And there were a total of over 10.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when you say that you had problems with them, did that mean some armed incidents taking place as well?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who with? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, someone might get drunk and start shooting round town and causing disturbances.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean of the refugees. Well, that was the general sort of thing that happened. There was sporadic shooting. Well, everybody shot. Daidza's men would shoot, our men would start shooting. Those were the times.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at document P 00952, please. You have the document, I think.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: P 00952 is the number. It is a document from the military police, the traffic military police, dated the 24th of December, 1992, and it is a report referring to Jablanica. We have a description of the different incidents that took place and I'd like to read out the third paragraph. Not the entire paragraph, but the beginning which reads as follows: "Linked to the throwing of hand grenades at Croatian facilities, pursuant to an order from Rasim Pilav, a caterer from Prozor, who is at the moment to be found on the territory of Jablanica with another 40 to 60 individuals also from Prozor, they were responsible, who had recently taken part in the fighting in Prozor." So tell me, did you hear of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And you've heard of Rasim Pilav, have you not?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the man well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Excellent. Let's move on. Tell me this now, please: I know that everybody ran wild at the time and did a lot of shooting, and I just happened to focus on the problems caused by the Muslim side because I know that you'll be better informed about those incidents than some other incidents. But when you -- and you have military education and training. The army sets up a check-point, right, in times of war at a given location? One of reasons for which a check-point is established -- I'm just asking a hypothetical here, regardless of which army sets it up, is to preserve law and order; is it not? And when I say this, I mean, the movement of persons, weapons, armed persons and so on. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, partially. Check-points were erected in order to control the entrance and exit of people and goods, not for public law and order.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that was a way of controlling public law and order.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, but not fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: May we have on e-court now the following document which is P 01121. These are instructions from the military police administration. It's been signed by the chief, Valentin Coric, but his deputy signed on his behalf. It's dated the 13th of January, 1993. I don't want to read through the entire document. Everyone can do that for themselves. But it concerns the prohibition of carrying weapons -- for weapons. If they're going to the battlefield or returning from the battlefield or, rather, they can only have weapons on that occasion. So can this be checked at check-points?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Concerned long-barrelled weapons. Can we now have a look at P 0195. P 01095. Again, it's an order from Valentin Coric, signed in the same way, dated the 11th of January, 1993, and it's prohibiting entry into the territory of the HZ and HB, and this concerns all foreigners whose intention is to join military units to engage in combat. And then they say how this order will be implemented. I want to know whether check-points could be used for such purposes too.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Excellent. Yesterday, you mentioned military obligation, work obligation, and it was said that there were deserters who even disguised themselves as women. I think that's how you said that they avoided their military or work obligation. One way for any of the sides to control the passage of individuals who were trying to avoid their military or work obligation was to have controls at check-points. Was that correct -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: When mobilisation is being carried out or when all those who are fit have to perform their military or work obligation, then I assume that without authorisation from the relevant authorities, they may not leave their place of residence.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they shouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So, it's necessary to issue such certificates and a check-point is a place at which these people could be controlled, could be checked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more question now with regard to the incident at the Aleksin Han check-point. As far as I have understood, on the basis of the documents -- you've read the documents. So have I. I don't want to go through all of them now. But Risovac was under HVO control. Aleksin Han, Ostrozac and Velacici was under the control of the Territorial Defence or the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So at the time of the incident, the Prosecution has shown you documents about that. Aleksin Han was under the control of the Territorial Defence or, rather, of the military police of the Territorial Defence. They controlled that check-point.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was the military police or not, but it was under armija control.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When those kidnapped soldiers got in contact from Split, then I believe that a representative of the MUP from Bosnia and Herzegovina went to collect them in Grude and the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They contacted them from Grude.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I then assume that all the information about that event was given by them to the individuals who went to pick them up, the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So did the BH MUP carry out an investigation into the event?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Should they have conducted an investigation?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And tell me, in 1992 and right up to March, 1993, regardless of all the incidents that we have mentioned and everything else, you in Jablanica, your military police and the HVO military police, tried to cooperate. You informed each other about incidents. You exchanged information. You reported on incidents.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were there together within 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you did cooperate?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know that in February and March there were even joint controls over the HVO military police and the Territorial Defence military police?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were several attempts to establish joint patrols.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I said in 1993. Could we now have the following document on the screen: 5D 02007. It's a report on the work of the HVO military police in Jablanica. The period is the 28th of February, 1993, up until the 3rd of March, 1993. We can have a look at the next page. The title is "Patrol service." Can you see the second page, sir? Second paragraph, and it says that at the time that a curfew was introduced, and it says as of 2100 hours, joint patrols have been carried out with members of the MUP and the military police of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: What it says in this document, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to go back to Prozor although Prozor isn't your primary concern, but the Prosecution asked you about Prozor, so I will too.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Try.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best. When you started testifying, on the first day of your testimony, you said that refugees from Prozor started arriving even before the conflict in Prozor broke out in October. There were women and children who arrived there, and they came because they were afraid because of the tense situation.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about one month prior to the conflict, 10 days?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around the 20th. Yes, the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague Alaburic has shown you some documents today, documents that relate to Prozor, and I would now like to ask you whether you are aware of the Alfa and Beta plans, which were plans for the defence of the municipality of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the Territorial Defence Staff in Prozor was in 1992, in September and October, let's say?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Was it Muharem Sabic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I couldn't remember. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll now show you two documents and then I'll ask you something about those two documents. Could we have the following on the screen, P 00430. You have it too. It's a defence plan for the municipality of Prozor. The date is -- it can't be seen clearly but I think it's the 1st of September, 1992. Let's have a look at the last two paragraphs which say the following: The first plan is ELIF, which will be implemented in cooperation with units from the HVO and in accordance with the attached document Alfa. The second variant is plan BE which will be implemented on independent basis or in cooperation with TO units from the neighbouring municipalities, and in brackets we have Gornji Vakuf, Konjic and Jablanica. And it also says: "In accordance with the attached document Beta." It's been signed. This document has been signed by the commander Muharem Sabic.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the interpretation. You can see Muharem Sabic's signature?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at the time that this document concerns there was no conflict in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: When you have a look at these two paragraphs that I've read out, plan Alfa and plan Beta, as someone who knows about military matters, it's obvious that the person who drafted this document referred to the Beta plan, and he had in mind the situation in which the HVO would become his opponents, whereas they had been his associates before.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now have a look at the following document: P 00687. I apologise. Your last answer hasn't been recorded. I think you said that this can be seen on the basis of the document?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report from the security and information service. It concerns a conflict between the HVO and the ABiH in the territory of Prozor. It's dated the 1st of November, 1992. We can have a look at the fourth paragraph. Can you please read it to yourself so I don't have to read it out. Everybody has the document. The fourth paragraph describes the plans Alfa and Beta. And let's have a look at the third paragraph from below, and this paragraph says units from other parts of Gornji Vakuf were included in this plan, and it also says units of the armed forces of the ABiH in Jablanica. Now have a look at page number 2. It's page 2 in English translation, too, the last paragraph in the English translation. It's the third paragraph in the Croatian version. It says the Private 2 unit of Rasim Pilav is trying make a breakthrough towards Krancici but is not succeeding in doing so. And then three paragraphs lower down it mentions the miserable fate of the action and then some fled towards Gracanica and others towards Jablanica. That's what it says here. When I mention the name Rasim Pilav, is that the person I mentioned a while ago in connection to the disruption in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the documents shown to you by my colleague Alaburic, if you bear them in mind, and if you bear the documents that I have just shown you in mind, in the action that the Territorial Defence of Jablanica did not participate in, and this concerned the breakthrough towards Prozor, was this action in fact the implementation of plan Beta -- could it have been the implementation of that plan?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first time I've heard about this plan, so I couldn't answer that question. I've never heard about such plans.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: But you heard that someone from Jablanica was supposed to go with a hundred or 150 men to Prozor before the 24th of October, according to the documents; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says. It's in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: But you heard that this should have been done but wasn't done; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I'd like to congratulate you because you did not overstep your time limit, and I'd like to extend my congratulations to you for that. Counsel Ibrisimovic, you have until a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My questions will relate to exclusively what the witness -- the answers the witness gave to the Prosecutor. I won't go beyond that scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Idrizovic, I'd like to start off by asking you the following: You told the Prosecutor that you became the top-ranking officer at a certain period of time in Jablanica. When was that? When did you become the top-ranking officer, the commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 28th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: How long did that go on for?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 21st of January, 1993. Until the brigade was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And after the 21st of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 21st of January, 1993, I -- and I said this before; you probably weren't following what I was saying. But anyway, I said that the staff remained with 200 men, and their sole purpose was to provide security for the facilities, and I told you the reasons for which the brigade was established, and from the previous documents that were shown here today it is evident what the command structure was like for the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And you remained the Staff Commander with those 200 men?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So you had your subordinates, and I assume that the 4th Corps was above you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now, these 200 men provided security for the most important features in town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: As the Staff Commander, I claim that you were highly well-informed about what was going on in Jablanica, and you said several times that your knowledge was limited when it came to events in Konjic, Sovici, Doljani, but you had to know what went on in your own house. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you had an officer who kept you informed about events that they -- it held briefings with the president of the municipality, the brigade commanders and so on.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had that kind of thing going on when the conflict started. Up until then that was less frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: But anyway, you learnt of all the important events that were happening in town, and you learnt of anything that might cause a problem, become a problem in town.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And one of those problems was the Jablanica museum; right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Asked by my learned colleague, and you didn't say this during your testimony, you said that the refugees were accommodated in the museum.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims together?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a prison or a collection centre for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was something like that. The military police company, first of all, of the 1st and of the 6th Corps, and then -- well, in fact they were down there as far as the prisoners of war were concerned. They were in charge of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, were they prisoners of war and refugees together? Because it's a rather large building.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us where the prisoners of war were put up and where the refugees were put up.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- perhaps you won't believe me, but I entered that facility only once during the four years of the war, and that was towards the end of the year, the end of -- or, rather, the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about it. You said you were well-informed.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where who was put up, all I know is that the Croat refugees were put up in this building that was a glass building, so you could see inside. They were glass partitions, and you could see that the Croat refugees, when you looked towards the entrance, they were to the left of the building, which is where the trophy room was. What could you call it now? Well, the museum exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far the museum is from your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about 4 to 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Jablanica is a small town. I assume that you pass by that way many times?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you, the refugees from Stolac and Capljina were put up in the hall on a raised -- on a raised level, in the cinema hall, and in other buildings. So all the available buildings and premises were used for that purpose, if you're talking about 1993. I'm not -- so 600 refugees were there. There was the military police and there was this prison probably where the prisoners -- HVO prisoners of war were put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Your headquarters was 45 metres away from the cinema; is that right? 400 to 500 metres away from the cinema; right? And the Croat refugees, where were they from?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were from Doljani.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now, asked by my learned colleagues, you said that there were perhaps a little more than 20 prisoners of war, something like that.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say what the exact number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That was what your answer was.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it might have been, but I'm not sure of the exact number. I it wasn't my job to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, where do you get this number from, then, this information from?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, millions of documents passed through my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it should be the military police who is in charge, the military police of the 6th Corps that is in charge of the prisoners of war, and this office for refugees should be in charge of the other refugees in the camp.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, from the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any civilians among the prisoners of war in that detention centre? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say, civilians among prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, I never went in there. Don't ask me that. I have no idea. I didn't like to go anywhere where people were being held and incarcerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to show the witness on e-court 6D 00035, the following document. We have a hard copy for the Bench. Would the usher like to come up and collect it and hand it to them, please. Can you see the document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The document is a military secret, strictly confidential, battalion of the military police of the 4th Corps, Jablanica, the 5th of August, 1993. The commander of the military police company was -- what was his name?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. I can't tell you. There were a lot of shifts in that military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So it says the military police battalion of the 6th corps and then we have a list of names. What does it say here? Subject is the list of persons -- you read it out, please. Read out what it says underneath the heading.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you to read it out, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm fully aware of this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Would you read it out, what it says? What does it say? A list of persons to be found in the SRZ Jablanica museum who were not members of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So we have a list of individuals from 1 to 87; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see on the screen. I can't see the last number on the screen. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I looked at the document. Among the 87 persons listed as prisoners of war, who were detained, 55 individuals were women. Perhaps you know some people from this list.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you now whether the department for refugees should have been responsible for these people? I claim that these were people detained in the Jablanica museum who were not refugees.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. What are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was a very precise one. We have a document here, apparently refutable, which establishes that in the town where you held the highest military post that 87 persons were held, of which 55 were women. What explanation can you give us with respect to the incarceration of these women? If they were refugees, why were they not at liberty? No, Mr. Scott, let the witness answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's an error in the transcript, Your Honour, but I'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military police wasn't supposed to deal with this. This wasn't part of their duties, and the people who were from Doljani or who were brought from Doljani to the museum weren't detainees. They hadn't been imprisoned. They had free access to other town. Naturally, they moved around freely everywhere. As to how they felt, well, that's a different matter. I don't think they felt good. It's not necessary to point that out. If some wanted to go out, well, that was up to them, but, this wasn't a facility they had been imprisoned in. Living conditions were very difficult, as was the case for everyone else. There's no doubt about that. So I'm surprised that the military police battalion compiled such a list and dealt with civilians, because there was a staff whose responsibility it was to take care of refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, what the error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There was either a translation or perhaps a transcription error. But on page 110, and I think it's left the live screen now, but at page 110 at line 9, at least it's put into the record, the question was put by counsel. I looked at the document, among the 87 persons listed as prisoners of war -- were detained, 55 were detained, 55 individuals were women. Your Honour, that's not what the document says. The top of the document, which counsel referred the witness, says people who were not members of the HVO. So I don't think it's a proper characterisation of the document by counsel or at least it was mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I wanted the witness to read this out, but I'll read it out aloud so the interpreters can follow. "It's a military police battalion, 6 Corps, military secret, highly confidential. Subject, list of individuals who are in the SRZ." This means the collection centre of prisoners of war. "The Jablanica Muzej, but they were not members of the HVO. This shows that they were civilians, and on the whole, the individuals concerned are women. I'm saying that these people are detainees and not refugees." I have one more question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic, could you clarify something. When you say "SRZ" in your language, this means centre for war prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It means collection centre for prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, have you been following this carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have some other documentation. If I have a chance, I'll come back to it in redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic, very briefly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more question. We received this document from the Prosecution. That's what I'd like to point out. And since Mr. Scott has just asked about the museum in Jablanica, I was just following up on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony, you said that you could speak about events up to the 15th of April, 1993, but that there were other people who were more capable of talking about the events after that date. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Is one of the reasons for that statement the fact that there is this document on the events in Jablanica museum in the collection centre?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look. The corps military police battalion, well no one had anything to do with that battalion. None of us had anything to do with that battalion. None of us had any control over the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you a question. You said you were well-informed. I'll now refer to a document Mr. Scott referred to P 09400. This is the chronology. If something of this kind happened in Jablanica, it should be included in the chronology, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, my document concerns the period up to the 15th of April. Have a look at the date on this document. You shouldn't mix up pears and apples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, unfortunately, as you can see, there are another two Defence teams who haven't had time for their cross-examination yet, which means that tomorrow, you will have to return for the hearing that will start at 9.00. But rest assured, the Defence teams have 30 minutes each, according to our calculations, so if the Judges aren't too talkative, everything should be over for you by 10.00. We will do everything we can to release you as soon as possible. I invite everyone to return for the hearing that will start tomorrow at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of November, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
